catalog_quote: Prominence In marked difference to European languages, perceptual difference between stressed and unstressed syllables is reportedly not so easy to establish in the languages of South Asia, and Assamese is no exception. Owing to this difficulty, there are also differing views on stress placement rules in Assamese. Notable views on this aspect are those of Kakati (1962), who accepts Grierson's (1895) description, where Assamese is said to follow the pan-Indian system of accenting the heavy penultimate syllable. Goswami (1966) differs from this view and opines that primary stress in Assamese is on the first or second syllable and never moves beyond the second syllable. Some acoustic correlates supporting this view, like low-rise in pitch and longer syllable duration were shown in Mahanta (2001). sweep_summary: Only one work surfaced (twice, under two Glottolog ids): the Goswami & Tamuli 2003 'Asamiya' chapter in Cardona & Jain, The Indo-Aryan Languages (pp. 391-443; chapter DOI 10.4324/9780203945315-10 — Crossref's '-19' DOI for it is wrong). No open full text exists (not on archive.org, HathiTrust or Open Library; T&F paywalled, abstract only; Google Books has no preview), but overlapping Google Books snippet searches reconstruct its entire §9 'Word Stress' paragraph (p. 409) and the dialect stress note (p. 404): primary vs. weak stress, non-contrastive in degree; 'the position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable'; Eastern/Central 'medial stress' vs. Western 'strong initial stress', with the medial stress 'optionally being shifted either to the first or the second syllable from the left, and never beyond'. This confirms the catalog's left-edge two-syllable window but is silent on the weight condition and adds dialect variation, so it refines rather than changes the weight-sensitive (tentative) coding; Mahanta 2012/2001 remain the deciding sources (and Mahanta 2007 LOT pp. 172-173 and Twaha 2017 §2.5, both held by the project and read, restate the same weight rule). Saved:, goswami_tamuli2003_gbooks/ (raw downloads). Acquiring the printed chapter is medium priority (would supply any examples and the full dialect passage). downloads went through direct URLs and the r.jina.ai reader.

new_statements.quote: There are two word stresses: (i) Primary stress /'/, and (ii) Weak stress, phonemically unmarked. There is contrast in position rather than degree of stress in a word as both the stresses do not occur in the same environment. The position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable. [p. 404:] Eastern and Central Asamiya have medial stress, whereas Western Asamiya has a strong initial stress. Owing to the influence of Western Asamiya dialect in recent times, the medial stress is optionally being shifted either to the first or the second syllable from the left, and never beyond.

new_statements.reading: Independent reference-grammar statement (Goswami is the senior Assamese phonologist whose 1966/1982 view Mahanta 2012 cites) that primary stress is confined to a left-edge two-syllable window (first or second syllable, 'never beyond') and is not contrastive in degree. It confirms the catalog's window and left edge but gives no weight condition (nothing about closed vs. open syllables) and no default, so it cannot decide quantity-sensitive vs. fixed on its own; the dialect note attributes 'medial stress' to Eastern/Central Asamiya (the standard's base) versus 'strong initial stress' in Western Asamiya, which is a hedge the catalog's tone/notes could carry. The catalog's deciding source (Mahanta 2012 with Mahanta 2001) is more explicit (initial default; sigma2 iff sigma1 light and sigma2 heavy) and stays the deciding source; Goswami & Tamuli is corroboration of the window only. Also re-read in this search of works with stress in the title, fully held by the project: Mahanta 2007 (LOT 173) pp. 172-173: 'Within the Assamese word stress system, main stress is always assigned to the initial syllable.. The second syllable is prominent if it is heavy and the first syllable is light. Otherwise the first syllable is prominent.. Heavy syllables never occur as primary stress bearing units beyond the second syllable' — restates the catalog rule verbatim (same author lineage), and Twaha 2017 (IITG thesis) §2.5 p. 2-27 says the same for both SCA and the Nalbari variety.

new_statements.quote: In SCA the stress placement rule is predictable: P-words, being sensitive to weight-to-stress principle, place prominence on a heavy syllable, though the default position for stress assignment is the first syllable. Heavy syllables do not attract primary stress beyond the second syllable (Goswami, 1982; Mahanta, 2001). It is syllable duration, rather than pitch value, that serves as the cue to this prominence pattern which is greater in case of heavy (bimoraic) syllables compared to light (monomoraic) syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statements (initial default, second syllable when heavy after a light first, never beyond the second syllable; attributed to Goswami 1982 and Mahanta 2001). Adds the phonetic cue (syllable duration, not F0) and the domain fact that word stress is invisible to intonation, which is assigned at the P-phrase level. It describes Standard Colloquial Assamese specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the first syllable; a heavy (closed, bimoraic) syllable attracts it, but only within the first two syllables, so a heavy second syllable takes stress and a heavy third or later syllable never does. The cue is duration, not pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The paper adds that word-level prominence is intonationally inert: a P-word gets no tone of its own, and the low pitch accent L* of a P-phrase always sits on the phrase-initial syllable regardless of the word-stress pattern (e.g. khaboloi keeps first-syllable word prominence but carries no pitch accent inside the phrase kɔmɔla khaboloi).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the two-syllable window ('Heavy syllables do not attract primary stress beyond the second syllable').
new_statements.identity_note: Twaha & Mahanta 2016 describes Standard Colloquial Assamese (SCA), the eastern-district variety (Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Sibsagar, Jorhat), with speakers from Sivasagar; Mahanta 2007 names no dialect and treats standard Assamese. Goswami & Tamuli 2003 (per the on-disk snippets, p. 404) distinguish Eastern/Central Asamiya (medial stress, the base of the standard) from Western Asamiya (strong initial stress). The index-1 open URL is a different book entirely (Sayendra Narayan Goswami, Asamiya Sahityar Katha, a literary history in Assamese).

new_statements.quote: The examples below in (270) show that stress is on the initial syllable. However, owing to quantity – sensitivity, if a heavy syllable immediately follows a light syllable, the heavier counterpart emerges as the prominence bearing unit. The second syllable is prominent if it is heavy and the first syllable is light. Otherwise the first syllable is prominent. Assamese follows a trochaic rhythm and therefore stresses the initial syllable. Heavy syllables never occur as primary stress bearing units beyond the second syllable. [...] Moreover, in trisyllables, heavy syllables have secondary prominence, and whenever a stress clash is imminent, it is averted by leaving a syllable unfooted.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress falls on the initial syllable unless the first syllable is light and the second heavy (closed: VC/CVC/CVCC, coda consonants moraic), in which case the second syllable is stressed; heavy syllables beyond the second never take primary stress. Feet are bimoraic trochees built from the left edge; vowel length is not phonemic so CVV plays no role.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Heavy syllables in trisyllables bear secondary prominence (examples (270g-h) [mɔ.rɔ.mɔ̀r] 'loved', [zɑ.zɑ.bɔ̀r] 'vagabond', grave accent on the final heavy syllable); a threatened stress clash is resolved by leaving a syllable unfooted.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is not sensitive to affixation; under prefixation stress shifts to the new initial syllable (p. 172). Phonetic correlate (p. 174, citing Mahanta 2002): a distinct low fall on the first syllable of an (LL) word, a plateau contour over L(H) words.
new_statements.identity_note: Twaha & Mahanta 2016 describes Standard Colloquial Assamese (SCA), the eastern-district variety (Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Sibsagar, Jorhat), with speakers from Sivasagar; Mahanta 2007 names no dialect and treats standard Assamese. Goswami & Tamuli 2003 (per the on-disk snippets, p. 404) distinguish Eastern/Central Asamiya (medial stress, the base of the standard) from Western Asamiya (strong initial stress). The index-1 open URL is a different book entirely (Sayendra Narayan Goswami, Asamiya Sahityar Katha, a literary history in Assamese).

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among the sources opened. Twaha & Mahanta 2016 and Mahanta 2007 (both records, indexes 2 and 3, are the same LOT dissertation) state the same rule: initial default, a heavy second syllable after a light first takes primary stress, never beyond the second syllable. The only tension is with Goswami & Tamuli 2003 (index 1, not openable from its listed URL, already in existing_statements from snippets): it gives a bare 'first or second syllable' window with no weight condition and a dialect remark that Eastern/Central Asamiya have 'medial stress' while Western Asamiya has 'strong initial stress'. Twaha & Mahanta cite Goswami 1982 for the weight rule, so the two lineages are treated by the authors themselves as compatible; the dialect hedge is worth carrying in the notes.

sources.quote: 9 WORD STRESS There are two word stresses: (i) Primary stress /'/, and (ii) Weak stress, phonemically unmarked. There is contrast in position rather than degree of stress in a word as both the stresses do not occur in the same environment. The position of the primary stress is either the first or the second syllable. There are two stresses at the utterance level: (i) Sentence stress /'/, and (ii) Emphatic stress /"/. Phonetically there seems to be no difference between the emphatic and sentence stress.
